transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose it’s the driving, really… though I’ve driven all my life, you know, even when Miami was nothing like it is now. But lately, when my car gets onto one of those long bridges heading toward Miami, I just—my chest tightens right up, and my hands grip the steering wheel so hard. I get this sudden feeling that I have to get off the bridge immediately, even though of course there’s nowhere to go. It scared me enough that I thought I’d better talk to someone.
Do these feelings ever come on suddenly when you are not on a bridge or driving?

I don’t think so… I mean, not that I’ve noticed. It’s really those bridges that set me off. Driving around town, going to the grocery store or to my daughter’s, I’m usually all right—though traffic these days is just something else, nothing like when we first moved down here. But no, I can’t recall it just happening out of the blue when I’m sitting at home or anything like that.
When you’re on one of those bridges, is the scariest part feeling trapped there and unable to get off quickly?

Yes, that’s it, I think. The moment my car gets onto one of those long bridges toward Miami, it’s like my body reacts before I can talk myself out of it—my chest tightens, my hands just clamp down on the wheel, and I get this awful feeling that I have to get off right then. Which is silly, because of course you can’t, you’re just stuck there until the bridge ends. Miami traffic used to be easier years ago, but those bridges now… that trapped feeling is what really frightens me.
Do you get this same trapped, panicky feeling in other places where it might be hard to leave quickly, like tunnels or elevators?

I’m not really sure… I don’t take tunnels much, and elevators, well, I mostly just use them if I have to, like at a doctor’s building. I can’t say I’ve noticed the same thing there. It’s funny, years ago I used to go all over Miami without thinking twice, but now I plan my routes around those bridges if I can. So… no, not that same feeling in other places that I can think of.
Have you started avoiding those bridges because of this fear?

Yes… yes, I suppose I have. I don’t like to admit that, because I was always the one making the plans, driving everyone around, you know. But lately I’ve turned down gallery openings, and a couple of birdwatching outings I would’ve loved to go on—there’s a group I used to enjoy, they know all the good spots—and even visits with my daughter, unless someone else can drive me over those bridges. It’s embarrassing, honestly. I don’t feel like myself when I have to arrange my life around it.
Do you feel the same fear when you are high up in other places, like on a balcony or in a tall building?

I don’t really know. I mean, I’ve been in tall buildings before, especially down in Miami years ago when we’d go to events or visit people, and I can’t say I remember having that same… reaction. Balconies, I don’t spend much time on them now, but I’m not sure it’s the height exactly. It’s hard to separate, because the bridges feel like their own thing to me.
If someone else is driving and you are just a passenger crossing one of those bridges, do you still feel that same fear?

Yes, even as a passenger I can feel it coming on. It’s really the bridge itself, I think. The moment the car gets onto one of those long bridges toward Miami, my chest tightens and I get this awful urge that we need to get off it right away… which is silly, because of course there’s nowhere to get off.

I’ll find myself watching the lane, the water, the distance ahead—oh, those bridges seem endless sometimes—and then I start thinking about how I used to drive that way without a second thought. But yes, whether I’m driving or not, that fear can hit right away.
When you think about crossing those bridges, is the height above the water the part that frightens you most?

Not exactly the height, no… I mean, I can see why you’d ask that, because you’re up over the water and there’s all that space around you. But it’s more the thought of driving over all that open water, being out there on the bridge.

I know perfectly well those bridges have been there forever, and people cross them all day long without a problem. My daughter tells me that, too, in her practical way. But when I picture it, the fear just feels so much bigger than the real danger. It sort of takes over, even though part of me knows it doesn’t make sense.
If you crossed the same kind of long bridge on dry land instead of over water, would you still feel afraid?

I think… if it were the same kind of bridge but not over water, maybe it wouldn’t get to me the same way. It’s that open water underneath and around it that seems to do something to my mind.

I know those bridges have been there for years, and goodness, people drive over them every single day like it’s nothing. My daughter says that all the time. But when I picture myself driving out there over all that water, the fear just feels so much bigger than what’s actually dangerous. I can tell myself it’s safe, but it doesn’t quite reach the part of me that panics.
Do you feel afraid when you are out on open water, such as on a boat?

I’m not really sure, honestly. I haven’t been on boats much—at my age, most of my “water” is looking at it from the car window or from a restaurant, you know? Years ago we may have gone out with friends, but I can’t quite compare it to those bridges.

The bridge feeling is so particular… the road stretching out, the water on both sides. On a boat, I don’t know that I’ve noticed the same reaction, but I also haven’t tested it much.
Do you feel afraid when you are near deep open water, even when you are not on a bridge?

I’m not sure I can say, really. If I’m standing near water, like at a park or looking out from somewhere, I don’t think I’ve noticed the same feeling, not like with the bridge.

Though, you know, I don’t go wandering around near deep water much anymore. My daughter is always telling me to be careful where I step, even just on uneven sidewalks. So it’s hard to separate what’s the water and what’s just… being cautious at my age.

But no, I can’t think of a clear time where just being near open water, not on a bridge, brought on that same fear.
If you had to cross that same stretch of water in a boat instead of on a bridge, would you feel afraid?

I don’t really know, to tell you the truth. I’m trying to picture it, and I suppose a boat feels like a whole different thing than a bridge. The bridge has that long stretch where you can see the water all around and you’re sort of stuck going forward.

But a boat… I haven’t really done that in so long, not enough to say how I’d react. My husband used to know someone with a little boat years ago, and I remember more about whether we packed sandwiches than how I felt on the water. Funny what sticks in your mind.

So I guess my answer is I’m not sure. I might be nervous, but I can’t say it would be the same fear as crossing the bridge.
If you had to cross a long bridge over water while walking instead of riding in a car, would you still feel afraid?

Yes, I think I would still be afraid. Maybe even more so walking, because you’re right there with it, aren’t you? All that water underneath and around.

And I know, in my sensible mind, those bridges have been there for years. People cross them every day, trucks and families and everyone just going about their business. My grandson used to say, “Grandma, it’s just a road,” and of course he’s not wrong. But when I picture being out over all that open water, whether I’m driving or walking, the fear just gets much bigger than what the real danger probably is. It doesn’t feel reasonable, but it feels very strong.
If you were safely standing on the shore looking out at a large expanse of deep open water, would you feel afraid?

Standing on the shore… I think I’d probably be all right, or at least not the way I am on a bridge. It’s the crossing over it that gets to me.

I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years, and plenty of people drive over them every single day without a thought. My daughter does, I’m sure, and she worries more about whether I’ve eaten lunch than about the bridge. But when I think about being out there, driving over all that water, the fear just feels much bigger than the actual danger. It’s not really sensible, I know that.
